items.title: Ocean Relief, Salinity, Temperature & Water Characteristics
items.body:
## In one line
The ocean floor is not a flat tub — it rises and dips like the land — and the water above it has three measurable kinds of property: physical, chemical and biological.

## Why it is asked
APPSC and UPSC set one-mark facts on the deepest trench, the average salinity figure, the thermocline, and the exact syllabus wording "physical, chemical and biological characteristics". Knowing the sequence of relief features answers most of them.

## The story — relief from the coast to the deep
As you move out to sea the floor steps down through a fixed sequence. Each step has a job: the shelf feeds the world, the trench holds the deepest point.

| Zone | Depth / character |
|---|---|
| Continental shelf | 0–200 m, gently sloping; richest **fishing grounds**, holds offshore oil and gas |
| Continental slope | steep edge from the shelf down to the deep floor |
| Continental rise | gentle apron of settled sediment |
| Abyssal plain | flat deep floor, 3,000–6,000 m |
| Trench | the **deepest** feature (Mariana Trench, about 11 km) — formed where one plate dives under another |
| Mid-oceanic ridge | underwater volcanic mountain chain where two plates pull apart |

## The three characteristics of ocean water (syllabus wording)
- **Physical:** temperature, salinity, density, colour, waves.
- **Chemical:** dissolved gases (oxygen O₂, carbon dioxide CO₂), nutrients and mineral salts.
- **Biological:** marine life — **plankton** (tiny drifters), **nekton** (active swimmers), **benthos** (bottom dwellers).

## Salinity and temperature, simply
- **Salinity** is how much dissolved salt the water carries. The ocean average is about **35‰ (35 grams of salt per kilogram of water)**, mostly common salt.
- It is **highest** in enclosed, hot, low-rainfall seas (Red Sea; the Dead Sea — an enclosed water body with high evaporation and no outlet — about 332 g/L) and **lowest** near the rainy equator, the icy poles and the Baltic Sea.
- **Temperature** falls as you go deeper and as you move from the equator towards the poles.

## Terms explained
- **‰ (per mille)** means "parts per thousand" — 35‰ means 35 parts salt in 1,000 parts water.
- **Thermocline** = the middle layer (about 100–1,000 m) where temperature drops sharply, separating warm surface water from cold deep water.
- **Zooxanthellae / plankton / nekton / benthos** — see the biological row above.

**The deepest trench of each ocean**

| Trench | Ocean | Why it is asked |
|---|---|---|
| Mariana Trench | Pacific | holds the Challenger Deep — the deepest point of all the oceans |
| Tonga Trench | South Pacific | the second-deepest trench on Earth |
| Puerto Rico Trench | Atlantic | the deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean |
| Sunda (Java) Trench | Indian | the deepest point of the Indian Ocean |

**Where salinity is highest and lowest**
Salinity is generally **highest in the subtropics (about 20°–30°)**, where skies are clear and evaporation is strong, and **lower near the equator** because heavy daily rain dilutes the sea. Enclosed water bodies in dry regions — the **Dead Sea** and **Lake Van (Turkey)** — are exceptionally salty. Salinity does **not** simply keep rising with depth; a sharp change with depth is called the halocline.

## Don't confuse
- **Abyssal plain vs trench:** the abyssal plain is deep, but the **trench is the deepest** of all.
- **Thermocline vs halocline:** the thermocline is a sharp change in *temperature*; the halocline is a sharp change in *salinity*.

## Remember it
Walk the floor seaward: **"Shelf, Slope, Rise, Plain, Trench"** — shallow fishing shelf first, deepest trench last.

## TL;DR
- Relief order: continental shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → trench / ridge.
- Shelf (0–200 m) is the richest fishing ground and holds offshore oil and gas.
- Deepest point = Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (about 10,935 m); trenches sit at subduction zones.
- Three characteristics: physical (temperature, salinity, density), chemical (dissolved gases, salts), biological (plankton, nekton, benthos).
- Average salinity about 35‰; highest in enclosed seas like the Dead Sea, lowest near equator/poles and the Baltic.
- The thermocline separates warm surface water from cold deep water.
keyPoints: Relief sequence: continental shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → trench/ridge.
Continental shelf (0–200 m) is the richest fishing ground and holds offshore oil/gas.
Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep ~10,935 m) is the deepest point on Earth; trenches form at subduction zones.
Ocean water characteristics: physical (temp, salinity, density), chemical (dissolved gases, salts), biological (plankton, nekton, benthos).
Average ocean salinity ≈ 35‰; highest in enclosed seas like the Dead Sea, lowest near equator/poles and the Baltic.
Thermocline separates warm surface water from cold deep water; temperature falls with depth and toward the poles.

items.title: Ocean Currents, Waves & Tides
items.body:
## In one line
Ocean water is always on the move in three ways — steady **currents**, wind-made **waves**, and the Moon-driven rise and fall of **tides** — and these movements set both coastal climate and the world's best fishing grounds.

## Why it is asked
Examiners love matching a current to warm/cold and to its ocean, and asking when spring and neap tides happen. One clear table of currents and one rule for tides cover almost every question.

## The story — currents
A current is a river within the sea. **Warm currents** carry equator-heated water towards the poles, usually along the **western edge** of an ocean; **cold currents** carry polar water back towards the equator along the **eastern edge**. Where a warm and a cold current meet, deep nutrient-rich water is stirred up, feeding plankton and so creating the great fisheries (Grand Banks; the Japan coast; the Peru coast).

| Current | Type | Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| Gulf Stream | Warm | North Atlantic |
| Kuroshio | Warm | North-West Pacific |
| Humboldt (Peru) | Cold | South-East Pacific |
| Benguela | Cold | South-East Atlantic |
| Labrador / Canary | Cold | Atlantic |

## The story — waves and tides
- **Waves** carry energy, not water, across the surface — the wind pushes them and each water particle just circles in place.
- **Tides** are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused by the gravity of the Moon (and, less so, the Sun) plus the Earth's centrifugal force.
  - **Spring tides** (the highest range) happen at **new moon and full moon**, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up and their pulls add together.
  - **Neap tides** (the lowest range) happen at the **first and third quarter**, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel.

## Terms explained
- **Western / eastern margin** = the western or eastern side of an ocean basin, not of a country.
- **Upwelling** = cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface.
- **Tidal range** = the height difference between high tide and low tide.

**Tidal bore**
A **tidal bore** is a wall of water that rushes **up a river mouth** during the rising tide, when the incoming tide is squeezed into a narrowing estuary (the Hooghly in India).

## Don't confuse
- **Spring tide has nothing to do with the spring season** — it means the tide "springs up" at new/full moon.
- **Warm current = western margin, cold current = eastern margin** of the ocean (easy to flip).

## Remember it
"**New and Full = Full tide (spring); Quarter = Quieter tide (neap).**"

## TL;DR
- Warm currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) flow poleward on western ocean margins; cold currents (Humboldt, Benguela, Labrador) flow equatorward on eastern margins.
- Warm and cold currents meeting (Grand Banks, Japan, Peru coast) make the great fishing grounds.
- Spring tides at new and full moon (alignment); neap tides at the first and third quarter (right angles).
- Tides are driven mainly by the Moon; the Sun's tidal pull is about 46% of the Moon's.
- The Gulf Stream warms north-west Europe, showing how currents regulate coastal climate.
keyPoints: Warm currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) flow poleward along western ocean margins; cold currents (Humboldt, Benguela, Labrador) flow equatorward along eastern margins.
Meeting of warm and cold currents (Grand Banks, Japan, Peru coast) creates the world's major fishing grounds.
Spring tides occur at new and full moon (alignment); neap tides at the first and third quarter (right angles).
Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity; the Sun's tidal effect is about 46% of the Moon's.
The Gulf Stream warms NW Europe, showing how currents regulate coastal climate.

items.title: Coral Reefs — Types, Conditions & Bleaching
items.body:
## In one line
Coral reefs are limestone ridges built by tiny sea animals (coral polyps) that can only live in warm, shallow, clear, salty water — which is why they bleach and die when the sea heats up.

## Why it is asked
Reefs appear as "which condition is NOT needed" questions and as current-affairs items on bleaching and India's reef sites. The growth conditions and the three reef shapes are the core facts.

## The story — what corals need and build
Coral polyps live in partnership with tiny algae called **zooxanthellae** that live inside them and need sunlight. That partnership only works in a narrow comfort zone:
- **Warm water**, about 20–21°C or more, so reefs are tropical.
- **Shallow, clear, sediment-free water** so sunlight reaches the algae.
- **Normal sea salinity** — corals die near big river mouths, where cold fresh water and silt arrive — so cold water rich in fresh-water river discharge is unfavourable.

As polyps die, their limestone skeletons pile up into reefs of three shapes:

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fringing reef** | attached directly to the shore |
| **Barrier reef** | separated from the coast by a lagoon (for example, the Great Barrier Reef) |
| **Atoll** | ring-shaped reef enclosing a central lagoon (common in the Pacific and Indian Ocean) |

## What goes wrong — bleaching
When the sea gets too warm or too acidic, corals expel their zooxanthellae, lose their colour and turn white — **coral bleaching**. If the stress lasts, the coral dies. In India reefs grow in the **Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands**.

## Terms explained
- **Coral polyp** = the tiny animal that secretes the limestone skeleton.
- **Zooxanthellae** = the sunlight-dependent algae living inside the polyp; they give the coral its colour and most of its food.
- **Lagoon** = the shallow stretch of water between a reef and the shore.

## Don't confuse
- **Barrier reef vs atoll:** a barrier reef runs alongside a coast with a lagoon between; an atoll is a ring with open sea around it and a lagoon inside.
- **Bleaching is loss of algae, not loss of the skeleton** — a bleached coral is still alive at first and can recover if the water cools.

## Remember it
"Corals need the **4 S's**: Sunlit, Shallow, Salty, Sediment-free — and Warm."

## TL;DR
- Corals need warm (about 20°C+), shallow, clear, sediment-free water of normal salinity.
- Three reef shapes: fringing (shore-attached), barrier (lagoon-separated), atoll (ring-shaped).
- Coral bleaching is the loss of the symbiotic zooxanthellae due to warming and acidification.
- Indian reef sites: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar.
keyPoints: Corals require warm (~20°C+), shallow, clear, sediment-free water of normal salinity.

items.title: Marine Resources, Ocean Energy & Blue Economy
items.body:
## In one line
The ocean is a store of food, minerals and energy, and the plan to use it sustainably — without wrecking the sea — is called the Blue Economy.

## Why it is asked
This note holds several ready one-markers: what polymetallic nodules contain, what OTEC runs on, the 200-nautical-mile EEZ, and the meaning of the Blue Economy — all recurring exam facts.

## The story — three kinds of resource
- **Biotic (living):** fisheries on the continental shelves, seaweed and marine biodiversity.
- **Mineral:** **polymetallic (manganese) nodules** — potato-sized lumps rich in **manganese, nickel, copper and cobalt** lying on the deep abyssal plains; placer sands (monazite, ilmenite); and common salt.
- **Energy:** **offshore oil and gas** (for example, Mumbai High) and gas hydrates.

## The story — ocean (renewable) energy
Three different ocean motions can each be turned into power:

| Form | What it runs on |
|---|---|
| **Tidal energy** | the rise and fall of tides across a barrage (potential: Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat, Sundarbans) |
| **Wave energy** | the kinetic energy of moving waves |
| **OTEC** | the temperature difference (about 20°C) between warm surface water and cold deep water |

## Blue Economy and the EEZ
- The **Blue Economy** is the sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, jobs and ecosystem health — spanning fisheries, shipping, tourism, energy and marine biotechnology.
- A country's **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)** reaches **200 nautical miles** from the baseline (under UNCLOS); within it the state alone may use the living and non-living resources. **India's EEZ is about 2.37 million km².**

Under the **Deep Ocean Mission**, the **Samudrayaan** project will carry three persons to a depth of 6,000 m in the indigenous submersible **MATSYA-6000** (see the Deep Ocean Mission note for details).

## Terms explained
- **OTEC** = Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion — a plant that uses the warm-surface vs cold-deep temperature gap to drive a turbine.
- **Barrage** = a dam-like wall across a bay or estuary that captures the tide.
- **EEZ** = the sea belt out to 200 nautical miles where a coastal state has exclusive resource rights (1 nautical mile is about 1.852 km).

## Don't confuse
- **Tidal vs wave vs OTEC:** tidal uses the tide's rise/fall, wave uses moving waves, OTEC uses the temperature difference — three different sources.
- **Territorial sea (12 nm) vs EEZ (200 nm):** sovereignty ends at 12 nm; resource rights run to 200 nm.

## Remember it
"Nodules = **Mn-Ni-Cu-Co**; EEZ = **200**; OTEC = **temperature gap**."

## TL;DR
- Marine resources: fisheries, polymetallic nodules (manganese, nickel, copper, cobalt), placer sands, offshore oil and gas (Mumbai High).
- Ocean energy has three forms — tidal (barrage), wave and OTEC (temperature difference).
- India's tidal-energy potential lies in the Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat and Sundarbans.
- Blue Economy = sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, jobs and ecosystem health.
- The EEZ reaches 200 nautical miles under UNCLOS; India's EEZ is about 2.37 million km².

items.title: Deep Ocean Mission & Samudrayaan
items.body:
## In one line
The Deep Ocean Mission is India's programme to explore and use the deep sea, and Samudrayaan is its headline project — the first Indian plan to send people 6,000 m down in an indigenous submersible.

## Why it is asked
It is a live current-affairs favourite: the launch year, the ministry, the submersible's name, the depth, and where it will dive are all testable one-markers.

## The story
- The **Deep Ocean Mission (DOM)** was launched in **2021** by the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)** to explore the deep ocean for resources and to build India's own deep-sea technology, supporting the Blue Economy.
- It is a multi-year programme with **six components**: a crewed submersible and deep-sea mining, ocean climate-change advisory services, deep-sea biodiversity survey, deep-ocean survey and exploration, energy and fresh water from the ocean, and an advanced marine-station for ocean biology.
- **Samudrayaan** is India's **first manned deep-ocean mission**: it will carry **three persons to 6,000 m** in the indigenous submersible **MATSYA-6000**, built by the **National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai**.
- Its target is to explore **deep-sea minerals (polymetallic nodules)** and biodiversity in the **Central Indian Ocean Basin**, where India holds an exploration site allotted by the International Seabed Authority.
- Succeeding would put India in the small group of nations with crewed deep-diving capability.

## Terms explained
- **Submersible** = a small crewed craft built to dive very deep and return (unlike a submarine, it needs a support ship).
- **MATSYA-6000** = the name of that submersible; "6000" is its design depth in metres.
- **NIOT** = National Institute of Ocean Technology, the MoES body that built it.
- **International Seabed Authority (ISA)** = the UN body that grants licences to explore the deep seabed in international waters.

## Don't confuse
- **Deep Ocean Mission vs Samudrayaan:** the Mission is the whole six-part programme; Samudrayaan is only its crewed-dive project.
- **MATSYA-6000 vs the ship Sagar Nidhi:** MATSYA-6000 is the crewed submersible; Sagar Nidhi is a research support vessel, not the diving craft.

## Remember it
"**MATSYA = fish; it carries 3 people 6,000 m down** for the Deep Ocean Mission (2021, MoES)."

## TL;DR
- The Deep Ocean Mission was launched in 2021 under the Ministry of Earth Sciences to explore deep-sea resources and technology.
- It has six components spanning deep-sea mining, a crewed submersible, ocean climate services, biodiversity, ocean energy/fresh water and an ocean-biology station.
- Samudrayaan is India's first manned deep-ocean mission — three persons to 6,000 m in the submersible MATSYA-6000.
- MATSYA-6000 is built by NIOT, Chennai, and targets polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin.
- The Deep Ocean Mission directly supports India's Blue Economy goals.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Coast, Fisheries & Marine Hazards
items.body:
## In one line
Andhra Pradesh has the longest coastline on India's east coast — a huge economic asset for fishing and ports, but also a front line for cyclones, storm surges and tsunamis.

## Why it is asked
AP-specific coast facts (coastline length, the only major port, fisheries leadership) and the 2004 tsunami are high-value, state-linked questions the APPSC favours.

## The story — the coast as an asset
- AP's coastline is about **974 km — the longest on India's east coast** and the second-longest of any Indian state after Gujarat.
- **Ports:** **Visakhapatnam** is the only major (Union-administered) port; important non-major ports include **Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Machilipatnam**.
- The **Godavari and Krishna deltas** create rich estuarine and marine fishing zones, making AP a **national leader in fisheries and shrimp/aquaculture exports** (through MPEDA).

## The story — the coast as a hazard
| Hazard | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Tsunami** | an undersea earthquake (2004: off Sumatra, magnitude about 9.1) |
| **Storm surge** | wind-driven sea rise during Bay of Bengal cyclones |
| **Coastal flooding / erosion** | storm surge over low-lying delta land |

## Managing the risks and the pollution
- **INCOIS (Hyderabad)** runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (since 2007).
- Marine pollution — plastics, oil spills, sewage and nutrient runoff (eutrophication), industrial effluents — is tackled through **Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) rules, MARPOL compliance and clean-coast (Swachh Sagar) drives**.

**Plastic — the pollutant asked most often.** Plastic and microplastic waste is a leading source of marine pollution. It is mitigated by reducing single-use plastics, better solid-waste management and beach clean-ups.

## Terms explained
- **Major port** = a port administered under the Union government; AP has one (Visakhapatnam).
- **Storm surge** = an abnormal rise of sea water pushed ashore by cyclone winds (different from a tsunami).
- **Eutrophication** = over-enrichment of water by nutrients (from fertilisers/sewage) that starves it of oxygen.
- **MPEDA** = Marine Products Export Development Authority; **INCOIS** = Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services.

## Don't confuse
- **Tsunami vs storm surge:** a tsunami is a seismic sea wave from an earthquake; a storm surge is wind-driven water from a cyclone.
- **Major vs non-major port:** Visakhapatnam is AP's only major port; Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram and Kakinada are large but non-major.

## Remember it
"AP coast = **974 km, 1 major port (Vizag), No.1 in shrimp** — and the 2004 Sumatra tsunami hit it."

## TL;DR
- AP's coastline is about 974 km — the longest on India's east coast (second in India after Gujarat).
- Visakhapatnam is AP's only major port; Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Machilipatnam are key non-major ports.
- AP is a national leader in fisheries and shrimp/aquaculture exports, aided by the Godavari and Krishna deltas.
- The 2004 tsunami (Sumatra earthquake) struck the AP coast; storm surges and coastal flooding are cyclone-driven hazards.
- INCOIS, Hyderabad runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre; marine pollution is managed via CRZ rules and clean-coast drives.

items.title: High-yield Facts — Counter Current, Chandipur, OMT & Water Distribution
items.body:
## In one line
A short cluster of high-yield facts that examiners recycle: why the equatorial counter-current flows east, the "vanishing sea" at Chandipur, the ocean-temperature monsoon predictor, and how Earth's water is shared out.

## Why it is asked
Each of these has appeared almost word-for-word in prelims papers, so they are easy marks once the reasoning is clear.

## The story — four facts explained
**Equatorial Counter Current.** The trade winds drive the North and South Equatorial Currents **westward**, so water **piles up on the western side** of the ocean. That piled-up water flows **back eastward** along the calm belt near the equator as the Equatorial Counter Current — it is caused by this convergence, not by a wind blowing east.

**Chandipur 'vanishing sea'.** At **Chandipur (Odisha)** the sea withdraws up to about 5 km twice a day at low tide, letting people walk on the exposed floor — the result of a very gentle shore slope plus a large tidal range.

**Ocean Mean Temperature (OMT).** OMT is the ocean's heat content measured down to the depth of the **26°C isotherm** (about 129 m) in the **south-western Indian Ocean** during **January–March**. Because this heat store is steadier than surface temperature, the **January–March OMT predicts** whether the monsoon will be below or above its long-term average.

**Global water distribution.**

| Store | Share of all water |
|---|---|
| Oceans (salt water) | about 97.3% |
| Ice caps and glaciers | the largest **freshwater** store (about 2%) |
| Groundwater | the next largest freshwater store |
| Rivers and lakes | a tiny surface fraction |

So the freshwater order is **ice caps/glaciers > groundwater > surface water (rivers and lakes)**.

## Terms explained
- **Isotherm** = a line (or depth) joining points of equal temperature; the "26°C isotherm depth" is how deep you go before the water cools to 26°C.
- **Trade winds** = steady winds blowing from the subtropics towards the equator.
- **Convergence** = water (or air) flowing together from two sides and piling up.

## Don't confuse
- **Counter-current direction:** the counter-current flows **east** even though the trade winds blow west — because it is a return flow of piled-up water.
- **Rivers/lakes vs groundwater:** rivers and lakes hold **far less** fresh water than groundwater.

## Remember it
"Fresh water ranking: **Ice first, Ground second, Rivers last.**"

## TL;DR
- The eastward Equatorial Counter Current comes from the piling-up (convergence) of the North and South Equatorial Currents on the ocean's western side.
- Chandipur (Odisha) is the 'vanishing sea' — the water recedes a few km twice daily, exposing the floor.
- OMT is the ocean heat down to the 26°C isotherm depth (about 129 m) in the south-west Indian Ocean, measured January–March.
- The January–March OMT predicts monsoon rainfall better than sea-surface temperature.
- Water split: oceans about 97.3%; freshwater order is ice caps/glaciers > groundwater > rivers and lakes.

items.title: The Five Oceans — Size, Depth, Deepest Points, Islands & Marginal Seas
items.body:
### The five oceans

**In one line**
**Oceanography** studies the oceans; geographers divide the connected world ocean into five — **Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern (Antarctic) and Arctic** — each with its own deepest point, largest island and marginal seas.

**The story**
Oceanography covers the physical and chemical properties of the seas, their origin and geology, and their life. The word **ocean** comes from the Greek **"Oceanus"** — an enormous river thought to encircle the Earth. Unlike continents, oceans merge into one another, so their boundaries are drawn by convention.

| Ocean | Size and depth | Deepest point | Other facts |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pacific** | **largest** — about **one-third** of the Earth's surface, bigger than all the land together; average depth about **4,280 m** | **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m — the deepest on Earth) | named "peaceful" by **Ferdinand Magellan**; contains the **International Date Line**; linked to the Indian Ocean by the Indonesian seaways, **Torres Strait** and **Strait of Malacca** |
| **Atlantic** | **second-largest** — about **20%** of the surface; average depth about **3,646 m**; shaped like the letter **"S"** | **Puerto Rico Trench** (~**8,376 m**) | named after **Atlas** (Atlantis Thalassa); opened when Pangaea (north) and Gondwana (south) broke up; holds **Greenland**, the largest island; contains the **Sargasso Sea**, the only sea **without a shore** |
| **Indian** | about **20%** of the world's water; named after **India**; the **warmest** ocean; land-locked on the north | **Sunda (Java) Trench** (~**7,450 m**) | **Madagascar** is its largest island |
| **Southern (Antarctic / Austral)** | around Antarctica, **south of 60°S**; fourth-largest (second-smallest) | — | stormy; the **Drake Passage** (Cape Horn to the South Shetland Islands) links it to the Atlantic and Pacific |
| **Arctic** | **smallest and shallowest** — about **1.3%** of the world's water; ice-covered in winter; **lowest salinity** | **Molloy Deep** in the **Fram Strait** | joined to the Pacific by the **Bering Strait** and to the Atlantic by the Greenland, Labrador and Norwegian seas |

**Marginal seas** (seas, bays and gulfs that are parts of the oceans)

| Ocean | Marginal seas |
|---|---|
| Pacific | Philippine, **Coral**, **South China**, **Tasman**, **Bering**, East China, **Okhotsk**, Japan, Yellow, Celebes, Sulu |
| Atlantic | **Caribbean**, **Mediterranean**, **Hudson Bay**, Norwegian, Greenland, Scotia, **North**, **Baltic**, Irish Sea, English Channel |
| Indian | **Arabian Sea**, **Bay of Bengal**, **Andaman Sea**, **Red Sea**, Java Sea, **Persian Gulf** |
| Southern | Amundsen, Bellingshausen, **Weddell**, **Ross** |
| Arctic | **Barents**, Kara, Laptev, Beaufort (our source also lists the Irish Sea — an error; it belongs to the Atlantic) |

**Don't confuse**
Largest island of the Atlantic = Greenland; of the Indian Ocean = Madagascar. Deepest Atlantic = Puerto Rico Trench; deepest Indian = Sunda (Java) Trench.

**TL;DR**
- Ocean from Greek "Oceanus"; five oceans: Pacific > Atlantic > Indian > Southern > Arctic.
- Pacific: one-third of Earth, avg 4,280 m, Mariana Trench, Magellan named it, IDL.
- Atlantic: S-shaped, avg 3,646 m, Puerto Rico Trench 8,376 m, Greenland, Sargasso Sea (no shore).
- Indian: warmest, Madagascar, Sunda Trench 7,450 m; Southern south of 60°S (Drake Passage); Arctic smallest, least saline, Molloy Deep.
keyPoints: Ocean comes from the Greek "Oceanus"; there are five oceans — Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
Pacific is the largest (one-third of Earth's surface), average depth ~4,280 m, named by Ferdinand Magellan; contains the Mariana Trench and the IDL.
Atlantic: second-largest, S-shaped, average depth ~3,646 m, deepest point the Puerto Rico Trench (8,376 m).
Greenland, the largest island, is in the Atlantic; the Sargasso Sea is the only sea without a shore.
Indian Ocean is the warmest; Madagascar is its largest island; its deepest point is the Sunda (Java) Trench (~7,450 m).
Southern Ocean lies south of 60°S; the Drake Passage joins it to the Atlantic and Pacific.
Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest, with the lowest salinity; deepest point Molloy Deep (Fram Strait).

items.title: Important Straits, Channels & Canals of the World (and around India)
items.body:
### Straits — the narrow gates of the oceans

**In one line**
A **strait** is a narrow water passage joining two larger water bodies and separating two land masses; a handful of them — Malacca, Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb, Gibraltar, Bosphorus — carry most of the world's sea trade.

**The story**
Exams ask two things about a strait: **which two seas it joins** and **which two lands it separates**. Around India the "Degree Channels" and the Palk Strait are favourites.

**Straits around India**

| Strait / channel | Joins / separates |
|---|---|
| **Palk Strait** | Bay of Bengal (Palk Bay) with the Gulf of Mannar; separates **India and Sri Lanka** (Adam's Bridge / Ram Setu lies here) |
| **Ten Degree Channel** | separates the **Andaman** Islands from the **Nicobar** Islands |
| **Nine Degree Channel** | separates **Lakshadweep (Kavaratti)** from **Minicoy** |
| **Eight Degree Channel** | separates **Minicoy** from the **Maldives** |
| **Duncan Passage** | between South Andaman and Little Andaman |
| **Coco Channel** | between the Andaman Islands and Myanmar's Coco Islands |
| **Strait of Malacca** | Andaman Sea with the South China Sea; separates **Malaysia** and **Sumatra** (Indonesia) — busiest strait for Indian Ocean trade |
| **Sunda Strait** | separates **Java** and **Sumatra** |

**Key straits of the world**

| Strait | Joins | Separates |
|---|---|---|
| **Hormuz** | Persian Gulf – Gulf of Oman | Iran – Oman (UAE) — the oil chokepoint |
| **Bab-el-Mandeb** | Red Sea – Gulf of Aden | Yemen – Djibouti/Eritrea |
| **Gibraltar** | Mediterranean – Atlantic | Spain – Morocco |
| **Bosphorus** | Black Sea – Sea of Marmara | European and Asian Turkey (Istanbul) |
| **Dardanelles** | Sea of Marmara – Aegean Sea | Europe – Asia (Turkey) |
| **Dover** | English Channel – North Sea | England – France |
| **Bering** | Arctic – Pacific | **Asia (Russia) – North America (Alaska)** |
| **Magellan** | Atlantic – Pacific | mainland South America – Tierra del Fuego |
| **Drake Passage** | Atlantic – Pacific (Southern Ocean) | South America – Antarctica |
| **Torres** | Arafura Sea – Coral Sea | Australia – New Guinea |
| **Bass** | Tasman Sea – Indian Ocean | Australia – Tasmania |
| **Cook** | Tasman Sea – Pacific | North and South Islands of New Zealand |
| **Taiwan (Formosa)** | East China Sea – South China Sea | China – Taiwan |
| **Korea (Tsushima)** | Sea of Japan – East China Sea | Korea – Japan |
| **La Perouse** | Sea of Japan – Sea of Okhotsk | Sakhalin – Hokkaido |
| **Florida** | Gulf of Mexico – Atlantic | Florida – Cuba |
| **Davis** | Baffin Bay – Labrador Sea | Greenland – Baffin Island |
| **Messina** | Tyrrhenian – Ionian Sea | Italy – Sicily |
| **Otranto** | Adriatic – Ionian Sea | Italy – Albania |
| **Mozambique Channel** | (Indian Ocean) | Mozambique – Madagascar |

**Canals** — the **Suez Canal** (1869) joins the **Mediterranean and the Red Sea**; the **Panama Canal** (1914) joins the **Atlantic and the Pacific**.

**Don't confuse**
Bosphorus (Black Sea side) vs Dardanelles (Aegean side). Ten Degree = Andaman–Nicobar; Nine Degree = Lakshadweep–Minicoy; Eight Degree = Minicoy–Maldives.

**TL;DR**
- Palk Strait: India–Sri Lanka; Ten Degree: Andaman–Nicobar; Nine Degree: Lakshadweep–Minicoy; Eight Degree: Minicoy–Maldives.
- Malacca: Malaysia–Sumatra; Sunda: Java–Sumatra; Hormuz: Persian Gulf–Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb: Red Sea–Gulf of Aden.
- Gibraltar: Spain–Morocco; Bosphorus and Dardanelles: Turkey; Dover: England–France; Bering: Asia–America.
- Torres: Australia–New Guinea; Bass: Australia–Tasmania; Cook: NZ islands; Suez (Med–Red Sea), Panama (Atlantic–Pacific).
keyPoints: Palk Strait separates India and Sri Lanka; Adam's Bridge lies in it.
Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; Nine Degree Channel separates Lakshadweep from Minicoy; Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.
Strait of Malacca separates Malaysia and Sumatra, joining the Andaman Sea with the South China Sea; Sunda Strait separates Java and Sumatra.
Hormuz joins the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb joins the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
Gibraltar separates Spain and Morocco; Bosphorus and Dardanelles are in Turkey; Dover separates England and France.
Bering Strait separates Asia and North America; Drake Passage separates South America and Antarctica.
Torres Strait: Australia–New Guinea; Bass Strait: Australia–Tasmania; Cook Strait: the two islands of New Zealand.
Suez Canal joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea; Panama Canal joins the Atlantic and the Pacific.

items.title: Waves & Tides in Detail — Wave Parts, Constructive vs Destructive, Tide Types & Tidal Energy
items.body:
### Waves and tides

**In one line**
Ocean water moves **horizontally** (currents, waves) and **vertically** (tides, upwelling); waves are energy moving through water, and tides are the twice-daily rise and fall caused by the Moon, the Sun and centrifugal force.

**The story — waves**
In a wave the **energy** moves, not the water: each particle only turns in a small **circle**. **Wind** supplies the energy; a breeze of **two knots or less** raises ripples, stronger winds make white caps. As a wave nears the beach it is slowed by friction with the floor and **breaks when the water depth is less than half the wavelength**. The **largest waves** are in the **open ocean**; **steep** waves are young and local, while slow, steady **swells** come from far away. Wave height depends on wind strength, duration and the **fetch** (distance over which it blows).

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Crest / trough | highest / lowest point |
| Wave height | trough to crest |
| **Amplitude** | **half** the wave height |
| Wave period | time between two successive crests passing a point |
| Wavelength | horizontal distance between two crests |
| Wave speed | measured in **knots** |
| Frequency | waves passing a point per second |

| | Constructive waves | Destructive waves |
|---|---|---|
| Weather | calm | storms, long fetch |
| Effect | **build beaches** (deposit) | **erode** the coast |
| Swash vs backwash | swash stronger | backwash stronger |
| Shape | long wavelength, low | short wavelength, high and steep |

**The story — tides**
A **tide** is the periodic rise and fall of sea level, once or twice a day. Irregular rises caused by wind and pressure are **surges**. The Moon's pull is the main cause (it is **more than twice** the Sun's tidal effect); **centrifugal force** creates the second bulge on the far side. The **tide-generating force** is the difference between the Moon's attraction and the centrifugal force; its **horizontal** component matters most. Tides are higher over **wide continental shelves** and lower at mid-ocean islands; **funnel-shaped bays** magnify them into **tidal currents** (the world's greatest range is in the **Bay of Fundy**, Canada).

| Tide type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Semi-diurnal** | two highs and two lows a day — the **most common** |
| **Diurnal** | one high and one low a day |
| **Mixed** | unequal heights — west coast of **North America**, Pacific islands |
| **Spring** | Sun, Moon and Earth in a straight line — **twice a month** (new and full moon) — highest range |
| **Neap** | Sun and Moon at right angles, about **seven days** after spring tides — lowest range |

At **perigee** (Moon nearest) and at **perihelion** (about **3 January**) tidal ranges are larger; at **apogee** and **aphelion** (about 4 July) smaller. The falling tide is the **ebb**; the rising tide the **flow** or **flood**.

**Importance** — tides are predictable, guiding navigators and fishermen; high tides let ships cross shallow **bars** at harbour mouths; tides **desilt** and flush estuaries; and they make electricity (Canada, France — **La Rance**, Russia, China, and **Sihwa Lake** in South Korea, 254 MW, the largest).

**Tidal energy in India** — methods: **floodgate dams**, **tidal barrages** across estuaries, and **tidal stream generators** (underwater turbines). India's coastline is over **7,500 km** (a 2024 re-measurement puts it at about **11,098 km**). Best sites: **Gulf of Cambay/Khambhat** (range up to **11 m**), **Gulf of Kutch** (**8 m**) and the **Sundarbans**. Projects: **Durgaduani** creek in the Sundarbans (3.75 MW, approved 2008 but delayed; another source says 3 MW), a **250 MW** plant planned in the Gulf of Kutch, and a 50 MW plant at **Mandavi** (Kutch).

**Don't confuse**
Swash (water up the beach) vs backwash (water back). Spring tides have nothing to do with the season spring.

**TL;DR**
- Waves move energy; particles circle; break when depth < half the wavelength; amplitude = half the height.
- Constructive (swash > backwash, build beaches) vs destructive (backwash > swash, erode).
- Tides: Moon > 2× Sun; semi-diurnal most common; mixed on N. American west coast; spring twice a month, neap 7 days later; ebb vs flood.
- Tidal power: Gulf of Cambay 11 m, Gulf of Kutch 8 m, Sundarbans (Durgaduani); Sihwa Lake 254 MW; Bay of Fundy highest range.
keyPoints: Ocean water moves horizontally (currents, waves) and vertically (tides, upwelling).
In waves the energy moves, not the water; particles move in circles; a wave breaks when depth is less than half its wavelength.
Wave amplitude is half the wave height; wave speed is measured in knots.
Constructive waves have a stronger swash and build beaches; destructive waves have a stronger backwash and erode.
Surges are irregular sea-level rises caused by winds and pressure, unlike tides.
Semi-diurnal tides are the most common; mixed tides occur on the west coast of North America.
The Moon's tidal pull is more than twice the Sun's; perigee and perihelion (3 January) give larger tidal ranges.
Ebb = falling tide; flow/flood = rising tide.
Tidal power sites: Gulf of Cambay (11 m range), Gulf of Kutch (8 m), Sundarbans (Durgaduani); Sihwa Lake (South Korea, 254 MW).
Bay of Fundy has the greatest tidal range.

items.title: Ocean Currents in Detail — Types, Causes, Gyres, the Full Current Table & Effects
items.body:
### Ocean currents

**In one line**
Currents are wind-driven at the surface and density-driven at depth; the Coriolis effect bends them into great **gyres** (clockwise in the north, anticlockwise in the south), and their warm or cold water shapes coasts, deserts and fisheries.

**The story**
**Surface currents** occupy the upper **400 m** and are driven mainly by **wind**; **deep currents** — the **thermohaline circulation** — are driven by **density** differences from temperature and salinity. Other causes are the **Coriolis effect** (gyres turn **clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern**) and the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.

**Gyres** are huge circular current systems formed by winds, the Coriolis effect and basin shape.

**Important currents**

| Ocean | Warm currents | Cold currents |
|---|---|---|
| Atlantic | **Gulf Stream** (from the Gulf of Mexico), **North Atlantic Drift** (mild Western Europe), **Norwegian**, **Brazil**, North and South Equatorial | **Labrador** (Newfoundland), **Canary** (NW Africa — Sahara), **Benguela** (SW Africa — Namib), **Falkland** (off Argentina) |
| Pacific | **Kuroshio** (Japan), **East Australian**, North and South Equatorial, **Equatorial Counter Current** (flows east) | **California**, **Peru (Humboldt)**, **Oyashio** (from the Arctic, along Japan), **Kamchatka**, Alaskan (source) |
| Indian | **Agulhas** (east coast of Africa), **Mozambique** (between Madagascar and Africa), South Equatorial, **Somali** (seasonal, reverses with the monsoon) | **West Australian**; the **Indian Monsoon Drift** reverses seasonally — clockwise in summer, anticlockwise in winter |
| Southern | — | **Antarctic Circumpolar Current** (West Wind Drift) encircling Antarctica; East Wind Drift near the coast |
| Arctic | — | **East Greenland Current**; **Beaufort Gyre** (clockwise) |

Meeting points: **Gulf Stream + Labrador** (Grand Banks off Newfoundland), **Kuroshio + Oyashio** (off Japan), **Brazil + Falkland** (off Argentina).

**Effects of currents**

| Effect | Example |
|---|---|
| Cool, foggy, arid **west coasts** in the tropics and subtropics | cold Peru, Benguela, Canary, California, West Australian currents |
| Mild marine **west coasts** in middle and high latitudes | warm North Atlantic Drift (British-type climate) |
| Warm, rainy **east coasts** in the tropics | warm Brazil, Kuroshio, East Australian currents |
| Fog and **drizzle** where warm and cold waters mix | **Newfoundland** |
| Rich **fishing grounds** — mixing replenishes oxygen and plankton | Grand Banks, North Sea, off Japan, Peru |
| **Desert formation** — cold currents dry the air; the hot deserts lie on west coasts between **15° and 30°** and are called **trade-wind deserts** | Atacama (Humboldt), Namib (Benguela), Sahara (Canary) |
| Fuel for **tropical cyclones** — warm water piled up in the tropics | western tropical oceans |

**Don't confuse**
Oyashio (cold) vs Kuroshio (warm) — both off Japan. Agulhas (warm, Indian Ocean) vs Benguela (cold, Atlantic) — both off southern Africa.

**TL;DR**
- Surface currents (upper 400 m, wind) vs deep thermohaline (density); gyres clockwise NH, anticlockwise SH.
- Warm: Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas, Mozambique, East Australian; cold: Labrador, Canary, Benguela, Falkland, California, Humboldt, Oyashio, West Australian.
- Somali current and Indian Monsoon Drift reverse with the monsoon; Antarctic Circumpolar Current rings Antarctica.
- Cold currents → west-coast deserts and fog; warm–cold mixing → fisheries and Newfoundland drizzle.
keyPoints: Surface currents occupy the upper 400 m and are wind-driven; deep currents (thermohaline) are density-driven.
Gyres turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
Warm: Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Norwegian, Brazil, Kuroshio, East Australian, Agulhas, Mozambique.
Cold: Labrador, Canary, Benguela, Falkland, California, Peru (Humboldt), Oyashio, Kamchatka, West Australian.
The Somali current and the Indian Monsoon Drift reverse direction with the monsoon.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current (West Wind Drift) encircles Antarctica.
Brazil and Falkland currents meet off Argentina; Kuroshio and Oyashio off Japan.
Mixing of warm and cold currents creates fog and drizzle (Newfoundland) and rich fishing grounds.
Cold currents help form trade-wind deserts on west coasts between 15° and 30° (Atacama, Namib).

items.title: Salinity & Temperature Details, Sea-bed Law and Marine Resources (ISA, Nodules, OTEC)
items.body:
**The story**

### Ocean properties, sea law and resources

**In one line**
Salinity is set by evaporation, rainfall, river inflow and ice; temperature falls with depth in three layers; and the deep sea-bed beyond national waters is licensed by the **International Seabed Authority**, where India holds a polymetallic-nodule site.

**Salinity — controls and extremes**
- **Salinity** = total dissolved salt in grams per 1,000 g (kg) of sea water (‰). Average about **35‰**. Lines joining equal salinity are **isohalines**.
- Raised by **evaporation**; lowered by **precipitation**, **river inflow** and **melting ice**; spread by winds and currents.
- Highest open-sea values: the **Red Sea** (about **41‰**) and the **Persian Gulf**; landlocked extremes: **Lake Van** (Turkey, about 330‰), the **Dead Sea** (about 238‰ — NCERT) and the **Great Salt Lake** (about 220‰).
- Lowest: the **Baltic Sea** (fresh river water, low evaporation) and the **Arctic Ocean**; the **Bay of Bengal** is less salty than the **Arabian Sea** because of the Ganga–Brahmaputra inflow.
- Salinity is highest around **20°–40°** (subtropical highs, clear skies), not at the rainy equator.

**Temperature — vertical layers**
1. A warm **surface layer** (about the top 500 m, 20–25°C in the tropics).
2. The **thermocline** (about 500–1,000 m), where temperature falls rapidly.
3. Cold **deep water** near 0°C down to the floor.
Surface temperature falls from the equator to the poles; Northern Hemisphere oceans are a little warmer (more land contact).

**Law of the sea (UNCLOS, 1982; in force 1994)**

| Zone | Width from baseline |
|---|---|
| Territorial sea | **12 nautical miles** — full sovereignty |
| Contiguous zone | **24 nautical miles** — customs, immigration, sanitation |
| Exclusive Economic Zone | **200 nautical miles** — exclusive resource rights |
| Extended continental shelf | up to **350 nautical miles** |

**Sea-bed resources**
- The **International Seabed Authority (ISA)**, headquartered at **Kingston, Jamaica**, grants exploration **licences** in international waters — **not** the "Global Ocean Commission" (UPSC 2021).
- **India** holds ISA licences — the first, for **polymetallic nodules** in the **Central Indian Ocean Basin** (about **75,000 km²**; India was registered as a "pioneer investor" in **1987**), and later one for **polymetallic sulphides** on the Indian Ocean ridges.
- **Rare-earth elements** occur in sea-floor muds and nodules in international waters (UPSC 2021).
- Other resources: offshore oil and gas (**Mumbai High**, **Krishna–Godavari basin** — also gas hydrates), placer minerals (monazite, ilmenite on Kerala and AP beaches), salt, and fisheries.
- **OTEC** needs a surface-to-deep temperature difference of about **20°C**; India's low-temperature thermal desalination (LTTD) plants at **Kavaratti** (Lakshadweep) use the same principle to make fresh water.
- Offshore wind: **Hornsea 2** (UK) is the largest operating offshore wind farm.

**The AP angle**
AP's coastline is usually given as **974 km** (a 2024 re-measurement gives about **1,053 km**). The **Krishna–Godavari basin** off AP is India's main deep-water gas and gas-hydrate province, and AP beach sands hold heavy minerals.

**Don't confuse**
ISA (licences) vs "Global Ocean Commission" (an advocacy body). Territorial sea 12 nm vs contiguous zone 24 nm vs EEZ 200 nm.

**TL;DR**
- Salinity avg 35‰; isohalines; Red Sea ~41‰; Lake Van, Dead Sea, Great Salt Lake extremes; Baltic and Arctic lowest; Bay of Bengal < Arabian Sea.
- Three temperature layers: surface, thermocline (~500–1,000 m), deep cold water.
- UNCLOS: 12 / 24 / 200 / 350 nautical miles.
- ISA (Kingston, Jamaica) licenses sea-bed mining; India's nodule site in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (~75,000 km², pioneer 1987); KG basin gas; LTTD at Kavaratti.
keyPoints: Isohalines join places of equal salinity; salinity rises with evaporation and falls with rain, river inflow and melting ice.
Red Sea (~41‰) and Persian Gulf are the saltiest seas; Lake Van, the Dead Sea and the Great Salt Lake are extreme lakes.
Bay of Bengal is less saline than the Arabian Sea because of river inflow; Baltic and Arctic are least saline.
Ocean temperature layers: warm surface (~500 m), thermocline (~500–1,000 m), cold deep water.
UNCLOS: territorial sea 12 nm, contiguous zone 24 nm, EEZ 200 nm, extended shelf up to 350 nm.
The International Seabed Authority (Kingston, Jamaica) grants sea-bed exploration licences — not the Global Ocean Commission.
India holds an ISA licence for polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (~75,000 km²; pioneer investor 1987).
Rare earth minerals occur on the sea floor in international waters (UPSC 2021).
LTTD desalination plants at Kavaratti use the ocean temperature difference.
AP coastline: 974 km (2024 re-measurement ~1,053 km); KG basin gas and gas hydrates.

items.title: For Mains — Oceans, Blue Economy & Marine Resources
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-V** (clause M5-5: development vs environment, resource depletion, climate change, natural disasters and resources). Answers should move beyond prelims facts to a **resource-vs-conservation** argument built on named initiatives and data.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Significance | EEZ about 2.37 million km²; Blue Economy spans fisheries, shipping, offshore energy, seabed minerals, tourism, biotechnology |
| Potential | polymetallic nodules (Central Indian Ocean Basin), offshore oil/gas, OTEC/tidal/wave energy, deep-sea biodiversity |
| Threats | over-fishing, marine plastic, oil spills, eutrophication, coral bleaching, sea-level rise, cyclones and tsunamis |
| Governance | UNCLOS, International Seabed Authority, Deep Ocean Mission (2021), Draft Blue Economy Policy, CRZ rules, MARPOL |
| Way forward | sustainable fisheries, marine protected areas, early-warning systems, circular economy for plastics |

## Data, bodies and schemes to quote
- **Deep Ocean Mission (2021, MoES)** and **Samudrayaan / MATSYA-6000** (three persons to 6,000 m).
- **India's EEZ about 2.37 million km²**; coastline about 7,516.6 km.
- **International Seabed Authority** exploration contracts for nodules and cobalt crusts.
- **INCOIS (Hyderabad)** Tsunami Early Warning Centre (2007); the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
- **Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water)**; the draft National Blue Economy Policy.

## The AP angle
AP's about 974 km coast (longest on the east coast), Visakhapatnam major port, Godavari–Krishna delta fisheries and shrimp-export leadership make it a natural Blue-Economy case study — balanced against cyclone/surge exposure and coastal erosion.

## Use in answers
- **Example:** cite Samudrayaan and the Central Indian Ocean Basin nodule site to show India's deep-sea self-reliance.
- **Quote/frame:** "the ocean is the next frontier of growth — but growth that drains it is self-defeating."
- **Diagram idea:** a two-column balance — *resource use* (minerals, energy, fisheries) against *conservation* (reefs, mangroves, pollution control) — converging on the Blue Economy.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-V (M5-5): frame as development vs environment, not a prelims fact dump.
Significance rests on India's about 2.37 million km² EEZ and the multi-sector Blue Economy.
Quote the Deep Ocean Mission (2021), Samudrayaan/MATSYA-6000, ISA nodule contracts and SDG-14.
Threats to balance: over-fishing, marine plastic, coral bleaching, oil spills, cyclones/tsunami.
AP angle: about 974 km coast, Visakhapatnam port and delta fisheries as a Blue-Economy case study.
